subject: physics
scope: PD-14: one claim (Ohm's law, I proportional to V, V = I × R) plus its condition (constant temperature); the filament is the bounded qualitative exception

sources.title: NCERT Class 10 Science
sources.section: Chapter 'Electricity', section 'Electric Current and Circuit' (ammeter in series) and section 'Ohm's Law' (V ∝ I at constant temperature; V/I = R; V = IR)

sources.title: NCERT Class 10 Science
sources.section: Chapter 'Electricity', section 'Heating Effect of Electric Current' (the electric bulb filament gets very hot)

nodes.statement: Find the current through a fixed resistor at a new voltage with V = I × R, and state that it holds at constant temperature.
For a conductor at constant temperature, the current through it is directly proportional to the potential difference across it.
The ratio V/I is constant for such a conductor; this constant is its resistance R, so V = I × R.
A bulb filament gets hot when current flows; its resistance rises as it heats, so doubling the voltage gives less than double the current.
nodes.reliability_note: NCERT states the constant-temperature condition (Ohm's Law) and describes the hot filament (Heating Effect); it does not state in one sentence that filament resistance rises with temperature. That is standard physics at this level but needs subject review. The claim stays qualitative: no lamp current number exists anywhere in this build (PD-16).

nodes.statement: Doubling the voltage always doubles the current.
nodes.why_wrong: Only while the resistance stays constant; a filament heats, its resistance rises, so the current rises by less than double.

nodes.statement: Voltage is described as the push that drives current, resistance as what holds it back, current as the flow the meter counts.
nodes.what_is_lost: Voltage is energy per unit charge; 'push' does not say how much energy each charge carries. Nothing is used up: the same current flows all round the loop.

nodes.statement: The resistor is treated as staying at exactly the same temperature at two, four and six volts.
nodes.what_is_lost: A real resistor warms slightly with current; the change is negligible here but not zero.

nodes.prompt: A ten-ohm resistor has two volts across it, then four volts. Find the current each time and compare.
steps: Twice the voltage, twice the current (ratio 2).
V ÷ I = 10 Ω at both points: the resistance.

nodes.stem: A ten-ohm resistor carries 0.20 A at two volts. At four volts, same resistor: more current, less, or the same?
Same ten-ohm resistor at six volts. What does the meter read?
